activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Cole arrived at the gym twenty minutes early because Coach Ruiz was posting the tournament roster on the bulletin board by the water fountain, and the posting happened at the final buzzer tonight, not tomorrow, not next week. Cole was eighth on the scoring list. Ninth place did not travel to the tournament. He knew the number eight the way you know a stitch in your shoe, and he had come to dread the walk past that board.

He found Aydin already at the concession stand, but Aydin was not buying anything. He was watching the small TV bolted above the popcorn machine, where the halftime show was replaying the regional track finals from Saturday. Aydin wanted to write for the school paper, and he had decided that sports stats were his way in, so he was filling a notebook.

"Look at this," Aydin said. On the screen, two runners crossed the line almost together. The replay froze there, then flashed the times. The silver medalist had lost by four hundredths of a second.

Cole's mother had watched that race live on Saturday and had said the same thing twice since: "She lost by less than a blink." Now Cole stood under the TV and looked at the standings graphic, first through eighth, one clean column of names.

"That's the thing about a ranking," Aydin said, chewing his pen. "It shows who's in front. It doesn't show how far."

Cole stared at the screen while the announcers moved on. First and second could be a hundredth of a second apart, or a whole minute, and the list would look identical either way. Then he thought about the bulletin board, and his stomach went tight. Eighth and ninth was a ranking too. He had no idea what the distance was.

He borrowed Aydin's notebook, flipped to a blank page, and started a small rebellion against the list itself. He wrote down every game score from the schedule taped to the wall, then every player's points from the team app on Aydin's phone. Aydin kept the numbers coming while they found seats in the bleachers, because the game would start in six minutes and the buzzer would come faster than either of them wanted. By the second quarter Cole had it: the seventh-place player was ahead of him by one point, and the ninth-place player was behind him by forty-one. The distance going down was huge. The distance going up was nothing.

At halftime he walked down to the bench during warmups and showed the page to Coach Ruiz. "I'm one point out of seventh," Cole said. "Not one point from getting cut." The coach read the page, looked at the scoreboard clock, and said, "Get back up there. We'll talk after." Anabelle, keeping the clock at the scorer's table, gave him a thumbs-up she usually saved for made free throws.

The home team won by six. When the buzzer sounded, Cole walked to the bulletin board with his heart going hard, Aydin a step behind with the notebook still open. The roster was up, his name in the traveling twelve. Below it, the coach had pinned a second sheet, the point totals, all fourteen players, every number distinct and printed in order. Two names near the bottom sat one point apart. "See," Aydin said, tapping them. "The list never tells you that."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: A swimmer caught in a rip current can usually escape by swimming parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, rather than straight against it.
story:
The beach was still two hours away, and Jasmine had read the safety card from the glovebox four times already. "Rip current," she said, holding it up so Laurence and Adalynn could see from the back seat. "That's what it's called when the water pulls you out away from the beach."

"Then you just swim as hard as you can back in, right?" Laurence said. He was plugging his phone into the charger, and when the screen stayed dark he muttered something about the voltage being too low.

"That's the conventional answer," Jasmine said slowly, "but listen to this." She read the card aloud. A swimmer caught in a rip current can usually escape by swimming parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, rather than straight against it. She frowned at the words. "So the pull is narrow. Like a river inside the ocean."

"That makes no sense," Adalynn said. "If something's dragging you out, you fight it. That's just obvious."

Jasmine looked out the window for a long moment, turning the idea over. Then she unrolled her part of the window halfway. The wind poured in as a strong, steady stream, and she held the card up in front of it. The card snapped backward, toward the back of the car. "Okay," she said. "The wind is the current, pulling toward the back. Watch." She slid the card sideways, parallel to the front seats, keeping it level. It still fluttered, but it moved smoothly across the window opening and out of the wind's path altogether. When she tried to push it forward, straight against the wind, the card buckled and jammed against the frame.

"Because it's narrow," Adalynn said, sitting up straight. "You only have to go a little ways sideways and you're out of it, but fighting it head on, it just keeps pulling."

"It's like the card found the edge of the wind," Laurence said. His phone finally buzzed awake, but he set it face down on his knee without looking at it. "So if the water ever grabs me, I swim along the beach, not toward it."

"Until you're out of the current," Jasmine said. "Then you swim in." She rolled the window back up and gave Adalynn the card, since Adalynn's little sister was meeting them at the hotel and would want to hear it too.

When they finally pulled into the lot above the sand, a red lifeguard sign stood at the top of the boardwalk steps. Jasmine leaned between the front seats to read it, then grinned at the two of them. "Same words," she said, and pointed. "Every word."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Viola Spolin's 1963 book 'Improvisation for the Theater' collected theater games and is often called the bible of improv teaching.
story:
Zachary was staying at his grandpa's house for the week, and on Monday the mail brought a letter from the community theater. The summer workshop was holding tryouts on Saturday, and one spot came with a scholarship that covered the whole fee. His grandpa read the letter twice and said he'd better practice, because the tryout was pairs improvisation and Zachary had never done it.

By luck, Dalton lived three streets over and was also trying out. They set up in the grandpa's garage, where two folding chairs stood in for a stage. Their first scene collapsed in about ten seconds. Dalton said, "We're on a pirate ship," and Zachary said, "No we're not, we're at school," and Dalton threw up his hands and sat down.

"You always cancel it," Dalton said. "Everything I start, you knock it down."

Zachary didn't argue, because it was true. He sat on an upturned bucket and thought. There had to be a rule underneath this, something you couldn't see but could test. Maybe every line had to keep the door open instead of shutting it. If Dalton offered a pirate ship, the move was to accept it and add something. He decided to classify each reply in his head before saying it: door open or door shut. Then he'd count which kind worked.

They ran it again. "We're on a pirate ship," Dalton said.

"Yes, and the captain just ordered us to scrub the deck," Zachary said.

Dalton grinned. "Yes, and the mop is missing."

"Yes, and I saw the cook steal it to stir the soup."

The scene ran four minutes, then six, then they were laughing too hard to keep going. It kept working. Whenever either of them started with no, the scene died, and whenever they started with yes, and, it grew.

That evening Zachary searched the theater's website and found a photo of their director, Mr. Ortiz, holding a battered paperback with a cracked spine. The caption named it: Viola Spolin's 1963 book, "Improvisation for the Theater." The site said it collected theater games and was often called the bible of improv teaching. Zachary wrote the title on a sticky note and put it above the garage sink.

The next day Mr. Ortiz himself stopped by the grandpa's house, dropping off flyers for Saturday. Zachary asked if he'd really learned from that old book.

"My copy is held together with tape," Mr. Ortiz said. "Negligent of me, the way I treat it. Show me a scene, and don't tell me no."

Zachary and Dalton stood up straight. "We're on a pirate ship," Dalton said.

"Yes, and the captain is watching us," Zachary said.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Moving the horizon line up or down changes the view: a low horizon makes the street feel seen from a child's height, a high one from a window above.
story:
Mr. Ong had set up easels in the middle of the gallery, right beneath a giant painting of an empty street that seemed to go on forever. "Today you learn one-point perspective," he said, tapping the canvas so that all the street's edges shot toward a single spot, like rain sliding down a window toward one crack. "Every line runs to the vanishing point. Draw your own street, any street, and make me believe I could walk down it."

Connor wanted his street to feel real, the kind you could ride a bike down. He sketched buildings, lampposts, a mailbox, and sent every edge racing toward a dot he had placed near the top of his page. When he stepped back, the street looked wrong, tilted, like it belonged to a giant peering over a rooftop. Across the table, Domenico was sprawled on the floor like he was napping, and his street looked wrong too, but wrong in the other direction, as if a bug were looking up from the gutter.

"Why is yours so tall?" Connor asked, crouching beside him.

"I don't know," Domenico said. "My dot ended up at the bottom. I just put it somewhere random." He shrugged, and his pencil rolled under the table, and he let it stay there.

Connor stared at the two drawings side by side. His dot sat high; Domenico's sat low. The gallery street painting hung above them with its own dot resting neatly in the middle, at exactly the height of a standing person's eyes. A suspicion tickled him like a feather. He flipped his paper over and drew a tiny stick figure at the edge of his street, then another on Domenico's. On his, the stick figure's eyes floated far below the dot. On Domenico's, the figure's eyes were way above it. The vanishing point, he realized, was like a hidden eye watching the whole street, and wherever that eye stood, that was the view you got.

He grabbed a fresh sheet and drew the same street twice. In the first, the dot sat low, near the bottom, and suddenly the street felt like being a little kid on the curb, the buildings looming like castle towers. In the second, the dot sat high, and the same street became a view from an upstairs window, small and far away, like a toy town. Ewan wandered over and squinted at them. "Those are the same street," he said slowly. "But the top one's from a window and the bottom one's from the curb. That's magic."

"It's not magic, it's the horizon line," Connor said, and he felt like a wizard anyway. He carried both drawings to the balcony above the gallery floor, laid them on the rail, and looked down at Domenico still sprawled by the easels. "Hey, Domenico!" he called. "Stay there! You're drawing the kid's view, so you have to stay low. I'll enforce it!"

Domenico saluted from the floor without getting up.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Garlic burns much faster than onion and tastes bitter when burnt, so many cooks add it only after the onions have softened.
story:
Muhammad curled his fingers into a claw and set the onion on the cutting board the way Ms. Tran had shown him, knuckles forward so the blade could only kiss them, not bite. Behind him, Colin banged through the restaurant kitchen's swinging door with a crate of tomatoes, and Dallas was already stirring the big pot like he thought speed was the whole job. "Sauce from scratch," Ms. Tran had said that morning. "You three, my station, Saturday prep. Mess it up and the dinner service pays for it." Muhammad wanted this. Two weeks ago he had talked his way into the weekend shift by claiming he could cook, which was true only if instant noodles counted, and every plate he sent out since had felt like a small lie.

He chopped the onion slow and even, eyes streaming, and it felt like real cooking. Then Dallas dumped the onion into the pan on high heat along with a whole spoonful of minced garlic, and the kitchen filled with a smell that went from good to sharp to something dark at the edges. When the sauce was done, Ms. Tran tasted it and frowned. "Bitter," she said. "Try it." Muhammad did. The tomato was there, but underneath it sat a burnt, acrid taste, like the shadow of the garlic had turned against the whole pot.

Colin blamed the tomatoes. Muhammad scraped a bit of the burnt garlic from the pan's edge and tasted it alone, and it was the bitterness exactly. He thought about the order of things. The onions had come out fine in the first minute, soft and sweet, so the problem had to be something that happened after that. The garlic, maybe, could not last as long as the onion on heat that strong. He looked at the pan, at the brown flecks, and tested his idea out loud. "Garlic burns faster than onion," he said. "Next batch, we soften the onions first, then add the garlic."

Dallas rolled his eyes but Ms. Tran only raised one eyebrow and said, "Make it." So they did. Muhammad chopped a new onion with his claw grip, steadier this time, and when the pieces turned soft and glassy, Colin slid the garlic in and stirred. The smell that rose was sweet and nutty, nothing dark in it. The sauce simmered, and when Muhammad tasted it he thought of the influential cooks on the cooking shows his dad watched, the ones who made order and timing look like magic. It wasn't magic. It was a rule you could find by being wrong first.

Watching the second pot bubble, Muhammad wondered whether he should have admitted weeks ago that he couldn't cook. Maybe. Or maybe the pretending was what had dragged him here, to this counter, on this Saturday, with a sauce that finally tasted right. "Narrator of my own story," he muttered, "and I get to decide what happens next." Dallas leaned over and stole a bread slice to dunk in the pot. "Then narrate me another bowl," he said, holding out the spoon.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: Rising action is the series of complications that raise the stakes and build tension before the climax.
story:
Katherine sat at the corner table of the school library with her draft spread in front of her, three pages about a girl who finds a dragon egg in her grandmother's attic. Jaycee had read it that morning and shrugged. "It's fine," she had said, which Katherine knew was worse than a complaint, because it meant nothing had happened to her while reading it. Now Katherine read it again herself, mouthing the words, and it did feel flat. On page one the girl found the egg, and on page two the dragon hatched and saved the village, and that was that.

She pulled a stack of books toward her, stories she loved, and laid them side by side. In one, a whole royal dynasty fell apart before the heroine ever picked up a sword. In another, the hero lost his map, then his supplies, then his best friend, before the final mountain climb. Katherine traced the pages with her finger and noticed that the big scenes did not come early. Each small trouble seemed to correspond to the next one, the way steps correspond to a staircase. The endings felt huge because of everything piled underneath them.

"Rising action," said Addyson, dropping into the chair across from her with two granola bars. "That's what Ms. Paquette wrote on my draft last month. See?" She flipped her notebook open to a margin note. "Rising action is the series of complications that raise the stakes and build tension before the climax. I got it wrong too. My story jumped straight to the flood."

Katherine looked at her own pages and marked the spot where the egg was found. "So mine needs trouble before the hatching," she said slowly. "She almost sells the egg. Then she breaks it a little. Then someone comes to take it." She wrote a number one, two, three in the margin, testing whether the order made sense, whether each problem grew from the last.

She rewrote until the librarian announced closing, then sat in the tranquil hush of the emptying room and thought about all the drafts she had given up on before, the ones she had decided were simply bad. Maybe they had only been missing their middle parts. She wasn't sure yet, and she folded that question into her backpack along with the pages.

At lunch the next day, Jaycee read the new version without looking up, and Katherine watched her shoulders tighten when the collector knocked on the grandmother's door. Jaycee reached the last line, set the paper down, and said, "Okay, now that one, I'd read the next chapter of that."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Ritardando, often written rit., means gradually slowing down, and accelerando means gradually speeding up.
story:
Georgia set her music on the rack in Ms. Vargas's studio and noticed the pencil marks right away. At measure twelve someone had written "rit." in small letters, and at measure twenty someone had written "accelerando." She had never played either one before.

"Those are mine from last week," said Pierre, who took the lesson before her and was still packing his books. "Ms. Vargas wrote them." He paused at the door. "Good luck with the ending. It's tricky."

Georgia started the piece, "Evening Parade," at a steady march tempo. When she reached the pencil letters, she kept going at exactly the same speed, because the notes themselves were not any harder there. From the hallway, she heard Pierre stop walking.

"Wait," he called back in. "Did you slow down at the rit.?"

"Why would I?" Georgia said. "The notes didn't change."

Pierre came back in and leaned against the doorframe. He looked like he was trying to decide something. "Half our band got that wrong too, at rehearsal on Tuesday. The clarinets slowed at measure twelve and the brass didn't, and it sounded like two different songs running into each other." He tapped the page. "Rit. is short for ritardando. It means gradually slowing down. And accelerando is the opposite. Gradually speeding up."

Georgia looked at the measure again. The march suddenly made sense to her, like a parade passing by and then coming back. She tried the passage, easing slower little by little through the rit., then pressing faster, bit by bit, into the accelerando. It felt strange at first, like walking uphill in sand, but by the third try her hands understood the shape of it.

"You know, I thought those marks were just decoration," she said. "I was sure speed was decided once at the top of the page and never changed." She had even told her mom that tempo markings at the start were the whole story. She would have to summarize it differently now: the composer could ask for a gradual change right in the middle, and the player had to answer.

Ms. Vargas came in, glanced at the clock, and smiled when she heard the last run. "Pierre, have compassion for my schedule and let Georgia breathe."

"Fine, fine." He hoisted his bag. "Play the ending for me before Thursday. I want to hear it right."

Georgia put her hands on the keys and began at measure twelve, slowing like a parade turning a corner, then gathering speed toward the final chord.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
story:
The bell rang, and Eve pulled her towel off the mirror in the locker room so she could look at her chin again. Three red spots had arrived overnight, like uninvited guests, and class photos were in exactly one week.

"New ones?" asked Arabella, tying her shoe two benches over.

"Three. My face is plotting against the photographer." Eve leaned closer to the mirror. "I don't get it. I wash my face every single morning. Why now? Why this year?"

Arabella shrugged. "Syed got a whole cluster last month. Ask him, he's the veteran of chin disasters."

Syed was pulling his gym shirt over his head at the far end of the row. "Hey, don't say my name and 'chin' in the same sentence," he said, walking over. "It's sensitive."

Eve turned around. "You read everything. Did you figure out why they happen?"

He dropped his voice like he was sharing a secret mission. "I did research. In puberty, hormones tell the oil glands in your skin to make more oil. The oil is called sebum. It clogs your pores, and that's what makes acne." He counted the steps off on his fingers. "So it's not dirt. It's oil. Inside my skin. That's why scrubbing until your face squeaks doesn't fix it."

Eve stared at him, and pieces started clicking together in her head. "So if I infer from that, the problem isn't the washing. It's what's underneath."

"Exactly. It's like blaming the mailbox when the mailman's the issue."

At the pharmacy that afternoon, Eve stood in the skincare aisle with Arabella and read labels like a detective. One bottle promised to blast away dirt with "micro-bead deep scrubbing." Another, a plain wash, said it worked on excess oil. She turned to Arabella. "The scrubby one attacks dirt. The sebum thing isn't dirt, it's oil. So this one's the match." She held up the plain wash, and a synthetic lemon-scented wipes pack as backup.

They tried it together, one morning at a time. Eve washed gently, once at night, once in the morning, and made herself stop poking at her chin even when it was extremely pokeable. Syed checked in daily like a coach. "Day four. Report."

"Some are fading," Eve announced on day six, angling her chin into the locker room light.

The morning of photos, she and Arabella stood side by side at the mirror. Two small spots remained, but the rest had retreated.

"Hair down to frame your face?" Arabella suggested.

"Hair down," Eve agreed. She grinned at her reflection. "Say sebum, everyone."

"Sebum," they chorused, and walked out to the gym.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977: the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation.
story:
The group chat, called Science Fair Squad, had forty-three messages before Emily even opened it. Nadia was typing in all capitals about the display board, Ilya had sent "fine" three times in a row, and someone had changed the group name to Science Fair Squad (Emily Is President). Emily read "fine" a fourth time and felt her face go hot. Ilya thought the whole project was a joke. Obviously he thought she was a joke too.

She typed "Do you even care about this??" and deleted it. Then she typed "What is your problem" and deleted that too. Instead she sent the plan again, with times: Ilya paints by Thursday, Nadia prints labels, Emily builds the volcano. Ilya replied "k."

"He's so rude," Nadia wrote. "Some people are just rude, that's all."

Emily stared at "k" for a long time. It was two letters short of a whole word. She was almost sure it meant he hated her, but almost sure wasn't sure, so she tried an experiment. She scrolled back through Ilya's messages from the past week, looking for a pattern. On Monday he had written real sentences, even a joke about magma. The "fine" and "k" started Tuesday afternoon. Something had changed, and it wasn't his personality, because nobody's personality changes on a Tuesday.

She asked Ms. Baptiste after class, the way you ask about a homework question so it doesn't count as gossip. "My brother left his psychology book on the kitchen table," Emily said, "and I was looking at it, and there was this thing where a guy named Lee Ross called something the fundamental attribution error in 1977."

"Interesting reading," said Ms. Baptiste, watering the fern that had never once done anything.

"So it's, like, people blame somebody's actions on their personality and don't think about their situation? Is that a real thing people do?"

"You'd have to ask the fern," said Ms. Baptiste, but she was smiling.

Emily went home and did the situation math. She messaged Ilya directly: "Are you okay? You've been sending one-letter answers since Tuesday." For a minute nothing happened. Then three dots appeared, and vanished, and appeared again.

"i got cut from travel soccer tuesday," he confessed. "i didn't want to tell the chat. everyone would do the sad face emoji. also my dad says i have to quit soccer anyway if my grades don't come up. also your volcano plan is actually good. i was going to paint tonight."

Emily put the phone down on her desk, screen up, so she could watch the chat from a polite distance. Then she picked it up again.

"New plan," she typed to Nadia. "We bring Ilya snacks on Thursday. Extravagant ones. Like a diplomat arranging peace between two countries, except the two countries are both Ilya."

Nadia sent back a single "k," which, Emily now understood, was sometimes a whole sentence.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: The body's sense of thirst weakens with age, so older people can become dehydrated without feeling thirsty.
story:
The train slid into the station at four minutes past three, and Piper spotted her grandmother through the window of the third car, waving with both hands. Piper waved back and squeezed past a man with a suitcase to reach the doors. Her grandmother stepped down carefully, hugged her, and said the ride had been fine except for the heat, which had followed her the whole way from the coast.

For the first two days of the visit, Piper noticed something she couldn't quite name. Her grandmother's water bottle, the pink one she carried everywhere, stayed full. At breakfast it sat untouched. At the park on Wednesday, the hottest day of the week, they sat on a bench in the shade and Piper drank half her own bottle while her grandmother said, "I'm not thirsty, love," and pointed at the ducks instead. Piper kept looking at the pink bottle. It was the same at dinner. Something was off, and Piper wanted to figure out what.

She tried an experiment on Thursday. "Grandma, I got you lemonade," she said, even though she had poured water with a slice of lemon, which was her grandmother's favorite. Her grandmother drank the whole glass. An hour later Piper brought a cup of tea, and that disappeared too. When Piper offered nothing, the pink bottle stayed full. It wasn't that her grandmother wouldn't drink. It was that she never felt the need. Piper called her friend Theodor, whose mother was a nurse, and asked whether old people got thirsty like everyone else. "Mom says no," Theodor said. "The sense of thirst weakens with age, so they can get dehydrated without ever feeling thirsty." Piper wrote it on the back of a receipt so she wouldn't forget.

She felt a quiet obligation now, something she couldn't ignore. At dinner she said, "Grandma, this is legitimate doctor advice from Theodor's mom. You have to drink even when you don't feel thirsty." Her grandmother laughed and said she'd been bossed around by better, but she picked up her glass. Mr. Rao, who lived next door and had come over to drop off tomatoes, nodded from the doorway. "My doctor told me the same thing last summer," he said. "I set an alarm on my phone now."

After that, Piper made it a small routine. Every couple of hours she filled the pink bottle and left it on the table beside whatever her grandmother was reading, no announcement, no fuss. Her grandmother began to say thank you less often, because it stopped being a favor and became just the shape of their days. On Sunday, Piper carried the suitcase to the station, and when the train pulled in beside them, her grandmother held up the bottle, empty at last. "Refilled it twice today," she said. "All by myself."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: After the climax, the falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends.
story:
The assignment from Ms. Paquette was due Monday, and Livia had brought it to her grandmother's house because Grandma's kitchen table was big and quiet and smelled like cinnamon. The problem was the story itself. Livia had a rescue scene where a girl named Jo pulled a lost dog out of a storm drain, and she had even fixed the dialogue, every quotation mark and comma in its place. But something still felt wrong, like a sweater with one sleeve inside out.

Macie had read the draft that morning in class and said, "The drain part was great, but then it just stops. What happened to the dog? Does Jo keep it? Does the owner show up?" Livia had no answer, because she honestly didn't know herself. She had been so busy getting Jo to the storm drain that she never thought about what came after.

She decided to test it like a science experiment. On a fresh page she wrote two endings. In one, Jo's neighbors turned out to be dog people with a fenced yard, and the notorious neighborhood cat, who had once stolen a whole roast off a porch, hissed at the new arrival from the fence. In the other, Jo's mom said they couldn't take the dog because their landlord would raise the rent, which Livia's dad called "basically a mortgage on a bungalow," and Jo had to track down the original owner. Then she read both aloud to Grandma, who shelled peas and listened with her whole face.

"The first one," Grandma said immediately. "That cat. I want to know if the cat wins."

"But the second one is more dramatic," Livia said. "There's a whole search."

"Darling, the big exciting part is over. You pulled the dog out of the drain. Now the story wants to settle, like soup off the boil. Show me what happens because of the rescue. Tie it up. Otherwise I'm left speculating about that dog all week." Grandma pushed the bowl of peas aside and added, "And I already speculate about your grandfather enough."

Livia laughed, then looked at her page and saw it. The climax was the rescue, and after the climax, the falling action and resolution had to show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends. That was the missing piece, and she hadn't needed anyone to hand it to her; she had just needed to hear a reader complain. She combined the endings: Jo kept the dog, the cat declared war on the fence line, and the girl who had lost him got a photo and visiting rights.

Monday morning she slid the story across the desk to Macie. Macie read to the last line and looked up. "The cat ambushed the dog with a pinecone?" she said. "Sequel. Definitely a sequel."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks; the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck.
story:
Eva knelt in the corner of the school garden, where the lettuce had failed and nothing grew but weeds. The spot looked desolate next to Ryleigh's blooming zinnias, but Eva didn't care about lettuce today. She cared about soup.

Two days ago she had set two jars of the same soup on her windowsill. One was sealed tight. The other she had covered with cloth, then lifted the cloth twice a day to "give it air." The sealed jar stayed fine. The open one turned cloudy and smelled like old gym socks. Something invisible had gotten in, and she wanted to know how.

"Ms. Farah-Ali says science fair projects need a hypothesis," Ryleigh said, dropping down beside her. "A testable guess. You write it down, then you try to wreck it."

Eva pulled her notebook from her back pocket. On the drive here, an idea had formed, and now she wrote it out big: The air itself makes food go bad. If that's true, soup kept in moving air should spoil even faster than soup in still air.

She had brought three jars of fresh soup from her grandmother's kitchen. Jar A she left open. Jar B she covered with cloth. Jar C she fitted with a strange twist of glass tubing she'd borrowed from the science room, a long neck bent into the shape of an S. Air could travel through the curve, but the trip was bendy and slow. She set all three on the flat stone by the garden fence and labeled them.

Every morning before class, she checked. Jace came with her on Wednesday, holding his nose at Jar A. "This one's a swamp," he said. Jar B had gone cloudy too. But Jar C, the one with the curving neck, still looked clean. On Friday it still smelled like soup. On Monday it was clear and golden, as if grandmother had just made it.

Eva stared at it. Her hypothesis said moving air should spoil the soup fastest of all, and instead the opposite had happened. She flipped through her notebook until she found the page from last week's reading, and her pencil stopped on a name: Louis Pasteur. He had boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks, and the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck. Not the air. The things riding on the dust. Her test hadn't wrecked her guess; it had flattened it.

She crossed out the old hypothesis and wrote the new one in careful letters. Then she capped Jar C and carried it to the science room, where Ms. Farah-Ali kept the garden club's voting jar for deciding what to plant next spring. Their little democracy needed a centerpiece.

"Ryleigh," Eva called across the courtyard, holding the jar up to the sun, "guess what's still soup."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In W. W. Jacobs's 1902 story The Monkey's Paw, Sergeant-Major Morris warns that the paw's wishes bring terrible results and throws it into the fire before the family rescues it.
story:
Noah sat at his grandmother's kitchen table with a photocopy of The Monkey's Paw and a highlighter that was already running dry. Ms. Wanjiru had said their book club discussion on Thursday had to include foreshadowing and symbolism, and Noah had underlined three sentences without knowing why, only that something about them felt important.

Jules slid into the chair across from him and stole a biscuit from the tin. "You look like the story bit you."

"I have to explain what the paw suggests, and I keep just writing 'it's a hand, hands do stuff.'" Noah pushed the paper across. "Help me."

Jules read for a while, lips moving. Then Jules stopped tapping the biscuit. "Okay, look at this part. The sergeant-major says the wishes bring terrible results. Then he throws the paw into the fire. Like he's trying to get rid of it before anyone can use it."

Noah grabbed the highlighter and circled those lines. The old man was warning the whole family before a single wish got made. It was like a sign on a gate saying danger, keep out, and the family walked in anyway. "That's foreshadowing," he said slowly. "The story warns everybody, and then the warnings come true."

They worked through the afternoon. Noah learned to isolate the moments where something small hinted at something big, like the wind rattling the gate early on, before anything bad happened. Jules pointed out that the changes in the story felt gradual, not sudden, which was maybe the point. "The paw itself is the symbol," Noah said, writing fast. "It looks like a lucky charm, but everything about it says the opposite."

Theresa arrived after dinner, and Noah presented his findings the way he planned to on Thursday. When he got to the fire scene, Theresa frowned. "Wait. If the soldier throws it in the fire, how does the family even get it?"

"The father snatches it out," Noah said. "That's the whole hinge of the story. Somebody was warned, somebody tried to destroy the thing, and they rescued it anyway."

Theresa leaned back. "So the family chose it. That's going to be a good argument."

His grandmother called from the doorway that it was getting dark and Noah should walk Jules and Theresa partway home. He gathered the marked-up pages, folding them into his pocket. At the gate, Theresa said, "Read us one part. The best one."

Noah pulled the pages out under the streetlamp and found the line where the sergeant-major warns them the wishes bring terrible results. He read it out loud, and the gate creaked in the wind behind them.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
story:
The group chat lit up at 8:47 on a Tuesday night, right when Kayla was supposed to be finishing her math homework. Miya had posted a ranking of the school softball team's hitters, and Kayla's name was third. Third. Behind Amanda, who had struck out five times last week alone.

"how is amanda above me," Kayla typed. "i get on base way more than she does."

Miya answered fast. "the ranking is by hits. amanda has 11, you have 9. numbers don't lie."

Kayla stared at the screen. The ranking counted hits, sure, but a walk counted for nothing in Miya's list, even though a walk got Kayla to first base just the same. She scrolled back through her own messages and started counting in her notebook, keeping meticulous tallies in two columns: hits and times she'd reached base without a hit. Walks, hit by pitch, an error she'd forced by laying down a perfect bunt. Nine hits, but seventeen times on base out of thirty-two plate appearances. She did the division twice. More than half.

Then she remembered Sunday, at her uncle's sports bar, the one with the sticky floors and the giant screens. He had leaned across the table mid-game and told her about the 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis. "It described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players," he'd said, tapping the table with each word. Then he'd gone back to his wings, and Kayla had filed it away without really hearing it. Now she heard it. Oakland hadn't had money. Everyone else had overlooked a certain kind of player. The number everyone trusted had hidden something.

She typed it out, trying to paraphrase her uncle without the chat thinking she was giving a book report. "ok so there's this book from 2003, 'Moneyball,' by Michael Lewis. it's about the 2002 Oakland Athletics. they used stats like on-base percentage to find undervalued players. on-base percentage. it counts walks."

The typing bubble appeared, disappeared, appeared again.

"wait," Miya sent. "you want me to redo the whole ranking?"

"yes. same games, same players, different number."

Amanda chimed in with a single row of laughing emojis, then, "do it, i want to see kayla go from third to first in real time." Kayla grinned and pulled up the team's stat sheet from the season page. Amanda had eleven hits but only fourteen times on base in forty plate appearances. Kayla did both players' math, checked it, and sent the results with a screenshot of her notebook so nobody could argue.

Miya's new ranking dropped at 9:15. Amanda second. Kayla first.

"verdict?" Kayla typed, before she could stop herself.

"fine. you win," Miya sent. "rematch saturday, and if you walk more than you hit again i'm ranking you by something else."

Kayla put her phone face down on her desk, picked up her pencil, and wrote seventeen out of thirty-two on the corner of her homework page, then drew a circle around it.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, the single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there.
story:
Sophie had a pencil, a ruler, and a piece of paper that was starting to look like a crime scene. Her assignment was to draw a street in one-point perspective, which meant every line of every building had to aim at one single dot that Mr. Szabó called the vanishing point. Hers was floating in the middle of the page like a lost freckle. Her buildings opposed the plan entirely; the left sidewalk sloped uphill while the right one dove off the edge, so her street looked like it was being folded in half by an invisible hand.

"I don't get it," she said to Coby, who sat across the kitchen table eating crackers he had not been offered. "The lines don't actually meet anywhere real. They just stop."

"That's the point," Coby said, crumbs commuting outward with every word. "The point that doesn't exist. You're drawing toward something that isn't there."

Sophie chewed her pencil. Mr. Szabó had told them one thing before the bell rang, something about Leonardo da Vinci, and she'd been too busy trying to find her eraser to catch all of it. She remembered a nail. That was it. A nail, in a painting, and it had made the whole class lean forward like one organism.

She looked up da Vinci's Last Supper on her mom's tablet, propping it against the sugar bowl. Christ sat at the center of a long table with his disciples spreading out on both sides, and once she searched, she saw it: all the lines of the ceiling and the walls ran inward, and where they converged was the head of Christ at the exact center. The whole room funneled toward him. It was like an equation she could suddenly solve; the room equaled all these lines, and the answer sat right there, calm, in the middle.

Then she found the sentence that made her sit up. A tiny nail hole was still visible at that spot. Leonardo had hammered in a nail and stretched strings from it as guides for his lines, strings he'd later pulled away, and the hole had outlasted five hundred years of everything else. Sophie stared at the screen. A nail hole, surviving in one of the most famous paintings on Earth, because a man had needed to aim his lines somewhere.

She grabbed her pencil again. At her vanishing point she pressed down hard and then harder, making a small dent in the paper, a real crater a person could find with a fingertip in the dark. Then she took a thread from her mom's sewing basket, pinned one end to the dent with a thumbtack, and stretched it toward the edge of the page. Wherever the thread lay, she drew her street. The buildings straightened like soldiers; the sidewalks ran out together toward the dot and vanished there, as instructed.

"That's cheating," Coby said, watching her trace the thread with an agile flick of the wrist, curve after curve.

"That's five hundred years of not being erased," Sophie said, and pinned a second string.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects.
story:
Alexa had been looking forward to the fire station field trip all week, mostly because rumor said they let you hold a real hose. The hose turned out to be heavier than a sleeping golden retriever, and by the time she set it down, her arms were shaking and Dalton was laughing so hard he had to lean on the truck.

"You'd drop a fire in two seconds," he said.

"You'd drop yourself in two seconds," said Alexa, which made Julia snort.

After the hose, Mr. Tse, their teacher, herded them toward a small glass case near the station's office. Inside sat an old leather helmet, a battered wooden bucket from the 1800s, and a folded paper poster about the great mill fire. Alexa leaned close and noticed a tiny dial fixed to the back wall of the case, with a needle that twitched now and then.

"What's that little clock?" Dalton asked. "Is it counting down to an explosion?"

The firefighter leading the tour smiled and said, "It's a humidity gauge. Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects."

"Paper swells?" Julia said. "Like a sponge?"

Alexa filed that away, and it came in handy that afternoon, because Mr. Tse had promised the class a treat: a chance to integrate what they learned by writing quiz questions for the younger kids they tutored on Fridays. The three of them sat at the station's picnic table with notebooks. Dalton wanted to ask, "How fast does a fire truck go?" Julia wanted to ask, "Why are dalmatians fire dogs?" Both fine questions, but Alexa kept thinking about the dial.

"Okay, here's a mystery," she said. "The captain's office had that antique wooden ladder propped right against the heater. If that gauge in the case matters so much, that ladder should be somewhere else."

"So?" Dalton said.

"So let's test it." Alexa borrowed a scrap of paper from the captain, wrote her name on it, and asked to tape it to the wall beside the radiator in the office, and a matching scrap in the cool hallway. The captain, who seemed delighted anyone cared, agreed.

They came back twenty minutes later. The hallway paper lay flat and smooth. The radiator paper had gone wavy at the edges, rippled like a chip.

"Whoa," said Julia. "It moved. It actually moved."

"So if that paper does that," Alexa said, "imagine a painting doing it every day for a hundred years. It would look like a potato chip."

Dalton, who had declared at lunch that old stuff was boring and museums were just rooms full of dust, flipped his notebook to a fresh page. "New question for my tutoring kid. Why does the museum keep the air weird for old paintings?"

"The air isn't weird," said Julia. "The air is sophisticated."

Dalton rolled his eyes, and Alexa reported her experiment to the captain, who promised to move the ladder that very afternoon.

"Tell your tutoring kids the fire station says thank you," he said, and shook her hand like she'd solved a real crime.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At the same yearly rate, interest compounded monthly grows a little faster than interest compounded yearly, because each month's interest starts earning sooner.
story:
Hazel stood by the cereal shelf at Marchetti's Grocery, holding two flyers she had pulled from the bank rack near the register. Both promised 3 percent interest on a savings account, but one said compounded yearly and the other said compounded monthly. She was saving for a used kayak that cost four hundred dollars, and she had exactly one year and a lot of babysitting money to get there, so the difference mattered.

"Tyrell, look at these," she said, grabbing his sleeve as he reached past her for the honey crunch. "Same rate. Same bank, even. Why would they print two ads?"

Tyrell squinted at the flyers. "Maybe one's a trick. Ads usually are." He turned one over, as if the fine print might be hiding on the back.

Cleo pushed her cart up beside them, chewing the free sample toothpick. "My brother says bank stuff is like a guild, all these secret rules nobody tells you." She leaned in. "Okay, wait. Yearly means they add your interest once a year, right? Monthly means they add a little piece of it every month."

Hazel's eyes went to the shopping list in her hand, but she wasn't reading it. "So if they add interest in March," she said slowly, "then in April, that interest from March is sitting in my account like it's my own money."

"And earning more interest," Cleo finished.

"That's logical," Tyrell admitted. "Each month's interest starts earning sooner than it would if you waited for the end of the year." He grabbed a pen from his backpack and the back of Hazel's list. "Let's collaborate on the math. If it's the same yearly rate either way, monthly should still come out a little ahead."

They worked it out right there between the cereal and the oatmeal, using the lid of a yogurt tub as a hard surface. Hazel did the monthly version, Tyrell did the yearly one, and Cleo checked every multiplication twice, because Cleo did not trust any of them, including herself. When they compared results, the monthly account had pulled ahead by a small margin, less than a dollar on Hazel's savings, but ahead.

"A little faster," Hazel said, staring at the two numbers. "Not by much. But faster." She thought about stretching her savings to five years instead of one, the way Ms. De Vries had suggested when she complained about the kayak price. The small margin would get bigger every year it sat there.

She folded the monthly flyer and tucked it into her back pocket, then steered the cart toward the dairy aisle. "Two percent milk," she announced, plunking it in the cart. "And a new savings account on Monday."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: A testimonial uses a famous or admired person to endorse something, even though that person may have no special knowledge about it and may be paid.
story:
The 42 bus smelled like rain and wet jackets, and Gabrielle had exactly nine dollars in her pocket, which was nine dollars short of the entry fee for the skate competition on Saturday. She had until Friday to find the rest, and so far her only idea was to sell the barely-worn sneakers in her backpack, the ones her aunt had mailed last month in a box with a famous player's face printed on the lid.

Guneet plopped down beside her, holding his phone so close to his face that the screen's glow turned his glasses blue. "Look," he said. "Deon Mack's new commercial. He says these are the best shoes he's ever worn. He laces them up and then he dunks, and the voice says every player in the league is switching over."

"Every player," Gabrielle repeated. The bus lurched around a corner and she grabbed the pole, the worn rubber of her own shoes squeaking against the floor. She was trying to picture every player in the league actually throwing out their old shoes at once, and the picture wouldn't come. It felt like when a magician says "nothing up my sleeve." Saying it didn't make it true.

"I'm getting them for my birthday," Guneet said. "My mom pre-ordered. Everyone at school is getting them." He said "everyone" the way you'd say "the sun rises," like a thing no one could argue with.

Gabrielle looked down at her backpack, where the same shoes, same red stripe, same swooping logo, sat folded in their tissue paper. Her pair was nearly new. If everyone really wanted them, someone on the bus might want to buy hers, and she'd have her entry fee. She stood up, cleared her throat, and held up one shoe. "Brand new," she said to the crowded rows. "Same ones Deon Mack wears."

A woman with grocery bags squinted at the shoe. "Does he, though?" said the man across from her. "My nephew works retail, and he says half the stars couldn't pick their own shoe out of a lineup. They get paid to say it."

Before Gabrielle could answer, the man by the back door looked up from his newspaper. He had grey stubble and a lanyard that read BUI, and he tapped the paper's full-page ad, Deon Mack mid-dunk, mouth open as if about to inhale the whole arena. "I photographed that shoot," Mr. Bui said. "Nice man. They flew him in for one afternoon, handed him the shoes, and he read the line off a card. He'd never seen them before."

Guneet's mouth opened and closed. "But he says they're the best."

"He says what's on the card," Mr. Bui said gently. "That's called a testimonial. Famous face, paid to praise it, whether he knows anything about it or not."

The bus hissed to a stop and half the passengers stood, and Gabrielle felt a strange, acute clarity, like someone had wiped the window she was looking through. The shoes in her hand hadn't changed, but the reason everyone wanted them had just shifted under her feet, and she watched Guneet stare at his phone as if it had lied to him personally.

"So nobody's switching over," Guneet said slowly. "The voice just says they are, so we'll feel left out."

"That part's called bandwagon," Gabrielle said, surprising herself with how steady her voice came out. She turned the shoe over, then held it out to the woman with the grocery bags, who had stayed in her seat. "They're good shoes anyway. Good grip, hardly worn. Fifteen dollars."

The woman looked at the shoe, then at her own cracked soles. "Ten," she said.

"Twelve," said Gabrielle, "and I'll throw in the box with Deon Mack's face on it." Somewhere behind them, Guneet slid his phone into his pocket.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
story:
Hudson sat cross-legged on Anya's living room floor, her phone balanced on his knee while she refilled the popcorn bowl in the kitchen. He was supposed to be sending the email inviting their whole class to her birthday party, but his thumb had stopped over the "To" line. If he typed thirty addresses there, everyone would see everyone else's address. Anya had told him last week that a boy named Laurent got teased after his address ended up on a giant class chain, and she'd said it quietly, the way she said things that mattered.

When she came back, he tilted the phone toward her. "If I put everybody in To, they can all see each other's addresses, right?"

"Right," Anya said, setting down the bowl. "My cousin called it a contact disaster once."

"Then what do I do?" Hudson scrolled through the compose screen, hunting. Below the To line sat a small grey link labelled Add BCC. He'd seen the word a hundred times and never once thought about it. Blind carbon copy, he read, in the little pop-up explanation. He tested the idea in his head: BCC people receive the message, but nobody else can see their addresses. If that was true, it solved everything. "Watch," he said, and typed Laurent's address into the BCC field, then his own, then Anya's, all thirty of them, one by one, while she read names off the class list.

He sent the message to himself first as a trial. A minute later his own phone buzzed, and he opened the test email and scrolled through it. The To line showed only his own address. Thirty people would receive the party invitation, and to each of them it would look private, almost personal, as if it had been written to them alone. No hidden list, no shared addresses, nothing opaque about who got it and who didn't.

"The BCC field hides everybody," he told Anya, holding up both phones so she could compare. "People in it get the message, but the other recipients can't see their addresses. So Laurent's safe."

Anya took her phone back and looked at the sent message for a long moment. "You know, my mom would've just pasted the whole list into To," she said. "You went and found the right door."

They sent the real invitation together, Anya pressing the button at the end so it would come from her account. Replies started arriving within minutes, and the first one was from Laurent: I'm in. Also, nice touch, I can't see half the class's emails for once.

Hudson grinned and let Anya generate the reply, a short message with the time, the address, and a note to bring nothing but themselves. She hit send, and somewhere across town, phones began to buzz.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish nouns have grammatical gender, so a male dog is "el perro" and a female dog is "la perra."
story:
Cole slid into the corner booth of El Sol, the restaurant where his class met every Thursday for Spanish dinner night, and pulled out his flashcards before his water glass even hit the table. "Tonight," he announced, "I'm describing my whole family in full sentences. Mom already signed the permission slip. I petitioned her for a week."

Rylee dropped into the seat across from him. "You petitioned your own mother?"

"It was a formal request. I wrote it out." He tapped his cards. "Tengo una hermana. I have a sister. Tengo un perro. I have a dog."

"You're doing yours already?" Esther hurried over with her menu and her notebook. "I'm stuck on mine. Our dog is a girl, Lulu, and I want to say she's the best, but I only know perro."

Cole frowned at his card. Perro. He'd written it in September, back when the class had just started, and he'd never once thought about it since. "Wait," he said slowly. "Remember when Mr. Hoffmann called on me and I said la mesa and he gave me that thumbs up? And Danny said el mesa and didn't get the thumbs up?"

"So?"

"So there's a pattern. El and la. Different words. They go with different nouns." He laid his cards out on the table like evidence at a trial. "If el mesa was wrong, then el can't just attach to anything. What if el and la split the nouns into two groups?"

Esther flipped through her notebook. "Mr. Hoffmann said el gato one time. And another time la mesa, la silla."

"Right, so la goes with mesa and silla. And el goes with gato." Cole sat back, feeling something click into place like a gear. "What if it's about the animal itself? A girl dog might not be el perro at all. It might be la perra."

"That sounds made up," Rylee said, but she was grinning.

"I'll test it." Cole shot his hand up. "Mr. Hoffmann!"

Mr. Hoffmann, who ran Spanish dinner night and was currently balancing three plates of tacos, raised his eyebrows from across the room.

Cole pointed at Esther's notebook, where she'd drawn a lopsided picture of Lulu with a bow on her head. "If the dog is a girl," he called, "is it el perro or la perra?"

"La perra," Mr. Hoffmann called back, "for a female dog. El perro is for a male dog."

Esther gasped like she'd won something. "La perra es mi mejor amiga!" she read off her freshly corrected sentence.

"Lulu is your best friend," Rylee said. "Bold."

"She carried my sock around for three days once. She's earned it."

The tacos arrived, luminous with lime and hot salsa, and Mr. Hoffmann set down a bonus plate of churros for the table. "For the student who figured out the groups," he said.

Cole grabbed a churro and held it up like a trophy. "Next week, the whole family," he said. "Every single sentence."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: An outline lists the main points and their evidence before drafting, so a writer can spot a weak or missing point before spending time on full paragraphs.
story:
Layla spread her materials across the kitchen table like a general planning a battle: the assignment sheet, two pencils, a granola bar, and a crumpled napkin she had brought home from her grandfather's house on Sunday. On the napkin, in his shaky handwriting, was an outline. Three points, each with evidence listed underneath. He had shown her how he planned arguments before writing, back when he wrote letters to the newspaper.

The assignment was due tomorrow, and she had chosen her topic: the school should replace its dying front lawn with a garden. She had a thesis statement ready, something she'd scribbled on her hand during math: "Our school should replace the lawn with a garden because it would save water, feed people, and teach students science." Three points. Sounded strong. She began copying the outline onto notebook paper, point by point, and under each one she wrote her evidence, exactly the way the napkin showed.

Point one was easy. She'd read that lawns need tons of watering, and a garden of native plants would diminish the school's water use. Point two went quickly too. The food bank on Miller Street took fresh vegetables, and the fourth graders already grew beans in cups on the windowsill. She wrote and wrote, her pencil scratching against the Formica, the kitchen smelling of onion from the pot simmering on the stove.

Then she got to point three. Teach students science. She tapped her pencil. What evidence did she have? She thought about the fungus unit in Mr. Sánchez's class, how they'd grown mold on bread in sealed bags, but that had happened in the classroom, not a garden. She checked her hand. She checked her notebook. Nothing. Her point three sat there with a big blank space underneath it, and something in her stomach went cold.

She picked up the napkin and looked at her grandfather's outline again. Under every one of his points, evidence. Every single one. That was the whole point of the outline, she realized: it showed the weak spots before you wasted an hour writing paragraphs. She had almost spent her whole evening drafting around a hole. Her heart knocked as she stared at the empty space, because the essay was due first period, and it was already dark outside.

Then she remembered. The district website had a page about a school across town with a pollinator garden, and it listed the lessons teachers had built around it. She grabbed her mother's laptop, typed fast, and there it was: a garden study cycle with math, science, and journaling. She wrote "district garden lessons, Bartlett Elementary" under point three and underlined it twice. Then she slid the napkin under her notebook, like a lucky charm, and started her first real paragraph. "Okay," she whispered to the empty kitchen. "Point one."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before, which can reveal that an old picture is being passed off as new.
story:
The rain had not stopped in two days, and everyone in Jack's class was talking about the river. Then Reagan sent him a message with a photo: a street turned into a brown river, a car half underwater, a porch light glowing just above the flood line. "This is by the school," she wrote. "They might cancel tomorrow."

Jack leaned closer to the screen. He did not recognize the street. That was the first thing that bugged him, because he had ridden his bike past the school a hundred times and never seen a porch like that, with a low stone wall and a crooked mailbox. He texted back, "Are you sure it's our school?"

"Viktor says it is," Reagan answered. "He got it from his cousin."

Jack despised being the last to know things, but he despised being fooled even more. Viktor had sent it to everyone in the group chat with the words BREAKING NEWS in capitals, and already three people had replied saying they would not do their homework tonight. It was reckless to spread something like that without checking, Jack thought, though he had done the same thing last month with a fake storm warning.

He tried zooming in on the photo, looking for a street sign, a store name, anything. The image was too blurry. Then he remembered something his older cousin had shown him once, late one night, when they were arguing about a picture of a shark swimming down a highway. Jack had laughed at the shark. His cousin had not.

He called Viktor. "Where did your cousin get that flood picture?"

"Some news page," Viktor said. "Why?"

"Meet me in the chat. I'm going to try a reverse image search," Jack said. "You can drag a picture into it and it shows where that photo appeared online before."

"That sounds fake," Viktor said, but he joined the chat anyway, and so did Reagan.

Jack saved the flood photo, opened the search page, and dragged the file in. The little bar spun. Reagan typed, "Well?" The bar kept spinning. Jack realized he was holding his breath, which felt silly, so he let it out and waited.

The results loaded. At the top was the same porch, the same half-drowned car, the same crooked mailbox. The page it came from was old, years old, from a town three states away, back when that street had actually flooded. Below it were more hits, other pages, other years, the same photo every time. Not our school. Not our river. Not this week.

Jack pasted the link into the chat. For a moment nobody typed anything. Then Viktor wrote, "Oh no."

"I almost told my mom we needed sandbags," Reagan said.

"Delete it," Jack typed, "before someone else thinks it's real." He could already imagine the photo landing on other phones, moving from chat to chat, the whole grade packing up for a flood that had happened somewhere else, long ago.

Viktor sent a single thumbs-up, and the BREAKING NEWS message disappeared from the chat.

Outside, the real rain kept drumming on the window, and Jack turned back to his screen to see if the river gauge was up.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals, and in a street scene they include road edges, curbs and rooflines.
story:
Maya spread her sketchpad on the picnic table in the backyard and checked her phone again. The community studio's street-scene contest closed at four o'clock, and it was already noon. She had drafted three versions of her street that morning, and every one of them looked flat, like buildings pasted onto paper instead of standing along a road.

Mr. Liu, who was weeding his tomatoes on the other side of the fence, leaned over and looked at her drawing. "Ah, perspective," he said. "My grandmother painted streets her whole life. She taught me one rule." He held up two fingers like fence posts. "The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals, and in a street scene they include road edges, curbs and rooflines." Then he went back to his tomatoes, humming, as if he hadn't just handed her the key to everything.

Maya stared at her drawing. Vanishing point, she understood; she had marked a dot in the middle of the page. But which lines ran toward it? She had only drawn the road edges slanting inward. She grabbed a fresh sheet and tried again, this time starting with the dot. From it, she ran her pencil outward. The road edges, yes. But the curbs too, the near edge and the far edge, slanting toward the dot on both sides. And the rooflines, sloping down toward it as the buildings stepped back. Even the shop awnings. It was like the whole street was being pulled by one invisible point.

A squirrel, some aggressive little rodent, darted across the table and knocked her eraser into the grass. Maya rescued it and kept drawing, because now the street was working. The buildings sat back from the road instead of standing on top of it. The road looked like it went somewhere.

Christina arrived at two, bike rattling, to see the entry before they biked it over together. "You didn't shade anything," Christina said. "Last year the winner shaded everything, all the windows, everything."

Maya looked at her clean, hard lines, the orthogonals ruling the page. For a second she doubted it, and she almost reached for her pencil to fill in the windows. Then she set the pencil down. "No," she said. "The lines do the work this time. If I shade over them, they'll disappear."

At the studio, the woman at the sign-in table held the drawing up and looked at it a long moment. "Nice orthogonals," she said.

Maya grinned at Christina. "Told you."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce an irritating gas, which reaches the eyes and makes them water.
story:
Aaron held the onion like it was a small bomb, which was pretty much how he felt about it. The soup for his family's dinner at the community kitchen had to be on the table by six o'clock, and it was already twenty past five. One chopped onion stood between him and the pot.

"Need help?" Hayley asked, sliding up beside him at the counter. Rafaelle was already peeling carrots at the far end, racing the clock and losing.

"I got it," Aaron said. He brought the knife down, and within four cuts his eyes were stinging and streaming. "Ow. Why is a vegetable doing this to me?"

Hayley grinned and handed him a paper towel. "You look like you just watched the saddest movie ever made."

"It's not funny." He wiped his face, but the tears kept coming. It was like the onion had a plan to humiliate him in front of the whole kitchen. He chopped faster, which made it worse.

"Wait," Rafaelle called over, squinting at them. "Why does it happen, though? Carrots don't do that. Why onions?" He held up a carrot like evidence.

Aaron stopped, eyes burning, and thought back to last Thanksgiving, when his grandmother had chopped onions at the sink wearing swim goggles. Everyone laughed at her, but she didn't cry once. He'd thought it was just a weird grandma thing. Now he wondered. She wasn't protecting her hands or her nose. She was protecting her eyes. So whatever the onion made had to travel through the air and land there. But how did cutting release anything? The whole onion just sat there, harmless, until the knife went through it. Something had to be locked inside.

"Maybe it's in the cells," he said slowly. "Like, the onion only becomes a problem when you break it open. The knife does it." He looked at Hayley. "So it's not the onion itself. It's what gets out when you cut it."

Mr. Hassan, checking the thermostat by the door, raised an eyebrow. "Soup by six, chef. Whatever theory you're testing, test it fast."

"Chill water," Aaron said suddenly. "Grandma kept a bowl of water next to her board." He didn't know why that would help, but the goggle memory made him trust her. He filled a bowl, dunked the onion halves, and cut the rest underwater, lifting them out only at the end. His eyes barely stung at all.

"That actually worked?" Rafaelle said, staring.

Aaron tipped the onions into the bubbling pot and grinned through the steam. "Grandma one, onion zero."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: The hongi is a traditional Maori greeting in New Zealand in which two people press their noses and foreheads together, symbolizing the sharing of the breath of life.
story:
The basement of St. Luke's smelled like cardamom and burnt coffee, because the interfaith welcome dinner always mixed everyone's food on one long row of tables. Avery had come with a jar of her grandmother's pickles, which was their household's rule for gifts: never arrive anywhere empty-handed. She was scanning the room for her friend Flynn when she saw the new family by the door, the ones who had just moved from New Zealand. Their daughter, Mathilde, was in her class at school.

A man from the new family stepped up to Mrs. Okafor, and then he leaned in and pressed his nose and forehead against hers. Avery froze. It looked like a head-bump, an accident, and she half expected both of them to apologize and rub their heads. Neither did. They stayed there for a second, close and unhurried, and then pulled apart smiling, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world.

Flynn appeared beside her, nudging a paper cup of punch toward her since her hands were full of pickle jar. "Did you see that?" he whispered. Avery nodded slowly. She had a theory forming, the way she did when a pattern showed up in math class. If it had been a mistake, it would have happened once. So she watched. When the temple's rabbi greeted the new family, it happened again, nose to nose, forehead to forehead. When the grandmother from the new family greeted Mathilde's teacher, Ms. Kamau, it happened a third time. Same gesture, every time, like a handshake that lived somewhere else on the body.

Avery tested her idea the only way she could think of. She carried the pickle jar over to Mathilde, set it down, held out her hand, and watched carefully. Mathilde shook it, ordinary and smiling. "Your family does the nose thing," Avery said, hoping that didn't sound abrupt. "What is it?"

"A hongi," Mathilde said. "It's a Maori greeting. You press your noses and foreheads together, and it means you're sharing the breath of life." Then she added, "Do you want to try it?"

Avery's stomach did a small flip, but she leaned in. Mathilde's forehead was warm against hers, and for one breath they stood there in the noisy basement, close enough that Avery could smell the cedar smoke that seemed to saturate Mathilde's coat. When they stepped apart, Flynn was grinning at both of them.

At dinner Avery noticed more than she ever had before. The new family waited until everyone at the table was served before eating, while Flynn's family said a quick grace, and Mrs. Okafor broke her flatbread and offered pieces around before touching her own plate. Nobody did it the same way, and nobody seemed to mind. Mathilde leaned over and pointed at the jar of pickles. "Is that a gift? We brought bread from home. My dad says you never visit anyone without bringing something to eat."

"Exactly," Avery said, and slid the jar down the table so it sat between them, half hers and half theirs, like a border nobody needed.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted.
story:
On Saturday morning, Ellie stood in Ms. Warsame's garage, where folding tables held boxes of donated food, and asked the question that had been bothering her since breakfast. "Why would a grocery store give away all these apples? They look perfect." She held one up like evidence.

Ms. Warsame, who ran the little food bank from her garage every weekend, just smiled and handed her a sorting chart. Archie, elbow-deep in a crate of oranges, grinned. "My dad says they dump stuff for the weirdest reasons. Too big, too small, too orange." Ellie rolled her eyes, but she persisted, turning each apple over, checking for the bruise or dent that must be hiding somewhere. Most of them had nothing. She stacked them in the "good" pile until it wobbled like a tiny red tower.

"Here's the thing," Archie said, balancing an orange on his head, which was his way of thinking. "My mom told me the U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted. Thirty to forty percent. Of all the food." He let the orange drop into his hand and popped it back in the crate. "So if we had ten of these, like, four would just vanish."

Ellie frowned at the apple tower. Ten apples, four gone. She grabbed a scrap of paper and drew it: ten circles, then crossed out three, then a fourth with a jagged line, right between three and four because nobody knew the exact number. She felt like a detective who couldn't see the crime, only the missing bodies. "Okay," she said. "So I want to test it. We weigh everything that comes in today, and we weigh what nobody takes by closing time. Like erosion, except it's apples falling off a cliff instead of dirt."

They borrowed the bathroom scale, which Archie claimed was inaccurate by exactly two pounds because it hated him. Ellie wrote numbers on the clipboard, quick and agile with the pencil, dodging Archie's attempts to add a zero. Ms. Warsame watched from her lawn chair, pretending to read but obviously eavesdropping.

At closing time, they did the math on the garage floor. Some zucchini had gone soft, a bag of spinach had wilted, and three loaves of bread sat untouched because everybody wanted the sourdough. Not quite four out of ten, but close, and Ellie circled the number twice. "Still a lot of apples falling off the cliff," she said. Archie picked up a leftover zucchini and brandished it like a sword. "Then we fight the cliff," he announced, and saluted the squash.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements that had not been discovered yet, and later discoveries such as gallium filled them.
story:
Eva wanted the last seat at the good lab bench, the one by the window, but Byron had claimed it by arriving five minutes early, and after a short negotiation she agreed to trade him her spare calculator for the period. She set her bag down beside him just as Ms. Virtanen taped an old, yellowed periodic table to the whiteboard. It looked wrong. Half a dozen squares were empty, and one of them had a question mark pencilled inside.

"Why does that one have a hole?" Eva asked, pointing. "Did someone rip it?"

Makai leaned over his binder. "It's not ripped. It's printed that way. My cousin has a poster like it at home."

Ms. Virtanen said only, "Nineteenth-century tables look like that. Work it out," and walked away to unlock the chemical cabinet.

"Great," Byron said. "She abandoned us."

Eva frowned at the poster. The empty squares sat in regular positions, whole rows where an element should have been. Around each gap, the neighbouring elements carried numbers in their corners.
